description: A round bale sits square in the hedge at the foot of the slope, its twine still intact, the flattened track it rolled down pressed clear across the pale bristled cut floor behind it.
A bale tipped up on its flat end stands like a drum on the pale bristled cut floor where the cut meets the dense green-gold wall of standing grass, wobbling on its tight spiral base.
A second bale has come to rest hard against the field gate, its twine snagged on the lowest bar, the gate swung open just enough to show how close the bale came to escaping altogether.
A wooden wagon heaped far too high with loose pale-green hay leans at the gateway, a slow avalanche of it sliding off the back end onto the pale bristled cut floor below, unhurried and continuous.
A wooden wagon piled high with loose hay stands at the open gate, a wooden rake laid flat across the very top of the load, and a tabby cat asleep along the rake handle, entirely at ease.
A flat-bedded wooden wagon heaped with loose hay lists hard to one side, three bales on top sitting at an angle, the whole load threatening the hedge with calm, unrushed inevitability.

A farm dog lies fully committed and flat in the one band of bale-shadow on the pale bristled cut floor, back legs stretched behind, one ear turned inside out, the bale above casting a clean hard edge of shade.

A scatter of sparrows works the pale bristled cut floor just behind a long combed ridge of raked grass, each one hopping and flicking stalks aside, the ridge dotted with the small quick shapes of them.
A hare sits up small and unhurried at the hard clean edge between the cut floor and the dense standing grass, its ears upright, the pale bristle behind it and the solid green-gold wall before it.
Four swallows cut fast and low across the open cut floor, banking hard at the abrupt edge of the tall standing grass, their wings nearly brushing the pale bristled surface on each low pass.
The whole air above the cut floor hangs thick with drifting hay dust and loose seed heads, every mote turning slowly, the cloud thickest above the combed ridges where the load has just gone through.

Hay dust rises from the cut floor in a broad slow billow, each mote lit and separate, thinning as it drifts toward the uncut side where the tall grass stands as a dense green-gold wall, dense and unmoving.
A long loose veil of hay dust and stripped seed heads hangs across the open cut half, thickest where the wagon track pressed the pale bristle flat, the dry soil showing through in a pale double line.
A straw hat sits crown-down on the flat end of a bale, a stone jar of water wedged in the shade directly underneath it on the pale bristled cut floor, beaded on the outside with cool damp.
A straw hat hangs hooked over the handle of a pitchfork planted upright in a loose heap of hay, the brim tilted, the handle casting a thin shadow across the pale bristled cut floor below.

A wooden hay rake stands upright in a long combed ridge of raked grass exactly where it was let go, the ridge combed tight and smooth on the left of it, loose and open and still unfinished on the right.
A farmer swings a full forkful of loose hay up over their own head onto a load already piled far too high, the forkful coming apart mid-arc and raining straight back down over them.
One farmer on the pale bristled cut floor pitches a great forkful up to a second farmer standing on top of the load, both leaning hard into the throw, the load swaying under the second one's feet.
A farmer walks the top of a heaped wagon with both arms wide for balance, the whole load shifting gently underneath, a straw hat left behind on a bale end far below.
A farmer rides the finished load flat on their back in the hay, both ankles crossed and one arm behind their head, while a cat sits upright at the very front like it owns the wagon.

A farmer stands still in the middle of the cut, the whole air around them packed with drifting hay dust and loose seed heads, every speck of it turning, a hare sitting up small at the edge of the standing grass entirely unbothered.
The farmer's shadow rakes enormously long right across the pale bristled floor of cut stalks from one side edge clean across to the other, the farmer small and upright at the shadow's root.
Three farmers sit along a great drum of hay tipped on its side, using it as a sofa, passing a chipped stone jar of water between them while a dog lies flat against the twine, entirely committed.

A farmer tips a stone jar of water straight over their own head and grins about it, the water scattering across the pale bristled floor of cut stalks in dark drops, a pitchfork stood up nearby in the bristle.
A farmer lies flat on their back in the one patch of bale-shadow, entirely on purpose, a dog pressing warm against their side, both of them ignoring the work completely.
